text: It's 5 in 10 of us who have badgered a woman who said no until she changed her answer. 8 in 10 of us who have lied to a woman in order to convince her to sleep with us. And more than 9 in 10 of us who have admitted to not accepting no as an answer. So we are back for Professor Neal's claims 3, 4, and 5. Quick recap. In video 1, he took a number from one university and applied it to all men. Hasty generalization. In video 2, he used the women's victimization rate as if it were the men's perpetration rate. Now for claims 3, 4, and 5, he says 5 in 10 of us badgered the woman until she changed her answer. 8 in 10 of us lied to convince her. And more than 9 in 10 of us did not accept no as an answer. Big claims. Scary numbers. But is there any support for them? Today, I'm going to cover claim number 3. So let's look at the study. The paper he shows is Isolate, Inebriate, Intimidate, Repeat by O'Sullivan and Ronis. Published in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence in 2026. Here's how the study worked. 2,689 men aged 18 to 34 were surveyed through an online panel called Qualtrics. They were paid $10 to fill out an anonymous online survey that took about 25 minutes. To be eligible, you had to identify as a man, be in that age range, and have had a sexual encounter with a woman in the past two years. That is the sample. Then the men were asked one main question. And the wording is important, so I want you to listen carefully. The question was, In the past four years, how many times have you used any of the following strategies to get or try to get a woman to have some type of sex when she didn't want to have sex or acted like she didn't want to have sex? Read it again. To get or try to get. So an attempt counts. Even if no sex happened. A guy who flirted with a woman, asked her out, got rejected, and respected that rejection, he can still be in this study if he used any of the 36 strategies during the attempt. Even if literally nothing happened beyond the conversation. And then when she didn't want to have sex or acted like she didn't want to have sex. So it includes cases where the woman actually didn't want it, but also cases where she just acted like she didn't want it. It could be soft nose, playing coy, saying, Oh, we shouldn't do it, while smiling. All of that could get coded the same way as a clear no. Now keep both of those things in mind because they matter a lot for what comes next. Now the men were given a list of 36 strategies and asked to mark how often they used each one. And here's the part that really matters. Those 36 strategies range from things that are clearly aggressive and predatory, like used drugs to help, used physical restraint, or threatened to hurt her, all the way to things that on the surface are much more ambiguous, like told her whatever she wanted to hear, or had a female friend around to make the woman feel safe and convince her. Those are very different categories of behavior, and the study lumps them all into one list of 36. Now here's what Professor Neil did. Out of those 36 strategies, he cherry-picked the ones that, when paraphrased a certain way, paint men in the worst possible light. Let's go through them. His third claim. 5 in 10 of us badger the woman who said no until she changed her answer. He most likely got this from the strategy, ask her repeatedly to have sex. 48.6% of men in the survey reported having done this at least once in the past four years. So roughly 5 in 10. But hold on. Merriam-Webster dictionary defines badger as to harass or annoy persistently. Now, is that what ask her repeatedly to have sex means? It can be, but it doesn't have to be. Remember what we just talked about. The question covers tried to get sex, including cases where she acted like she didn't want it. Let me give you a real-world example. Imagine you met a woman at a bar. You hit it off. You're vibing. You're making out. You say, want to come back to my place? She smiles and says, oh, you playboy. You think I will jump into your bed just like that? We don't know each other that well yet. Okay, you keep having a good time. The vibe is still good. One hour later, you say, you sure you don't want to come over? She smiles and says, okay, you go to your place and spend the night together. By the survey's wording, that would count. You basically asked her repeatedly to have sex, and she initially acted like she didn't want to. But is that badgering? Is that harassment? No. That is just how flirting works. Or imagine this. You asked her to come over. She said no. You asked again later. She said no. You respected it and went home alone. You never had sex. By the survey wording, that also counts, because you tried to get her to have sex, and she didn't want to. So here, a guy who got rejected and respected the rejection is still in this statistic. And the survey itself shows that in 35% of those cases, no sex actually occurred. Can the same item also capture genuine harassment, where a guy keeps pressuring a woman until she gives in just to make him stop? Yes, absolutely. And if it does, that is a horrible behavior and a real problem. But then there are other much more specific items on the survey for that, like gradually pushed verbally or physically until you got what you wanted. Those items exist precisely because they capture the actual badgering until the woman changes her answer. So when Professor Neil takes the broad ask her repeatedly item and paraphrases it as badgered until she changed her answer, he's not just reporting the data. He's misrepresenting it. He's picking the most aggressive possible interpretation of an ambiguous item, ignoring the fact that the item itself includes everything from rejected flirting to actual harassment and presenting it as if that is what the number means.
